idiom_name: EnvironmentKey + .environment(...) for state down, PreferenceKey for values up, generic containers for child content
implementation_notes: SwiftUI supplies both directions of implicit sharing: a parent injects state with .environment(\.key, value) and any descendant reads it through @Environment, which re-reads when the value changes, while a PreferenceKey lets children report values upward - Apple's documentation states that a view with multiple children automatically combines its values for a given preference into a single value visible to its ancestors - which is how containers collect child state or measurements. Generic container views take their children as a @ViewBuilder closure, so the call site decides the content and the parent decides behaviour. The classic JSX tricks are unnecessary; the price is that a missing environment value silently falls back to its default.
pitfalls: An environment default of nil/empty makes a misplaced child render as if a parent existed - prefer a default that traps in debug builds, or an @EnvironmentObject that fails loudly.
Children must read the environment with @Environment (a computed lookup), not capture it in a stored let, or they keep the value from the first render.
Preference aggregation runs bottom-up and merges via the key's reduce; a reduce that keeps only the last value silently drops siblings.
Environment propagation is per view identity - re-parenting a view (ForEach, sheets, navigation) can detach it from the injection point.

variants.name: UIKit: container view controller owning child views and their state
variants.implementation_notes: UIKit is the imperative retained-mode counterpart: a container view controller (or a custom UIView/UIStackView subclass) owns the family's state, and its children declare themselves by being added (addChild, addArrangedSubview) and by reading the parent's model object; changes travel back through delegates, target-action or a closure the parent supplies, and the parent updates each child's selected flag in the same pass. There is no automatic re-render, so the parent must set the child state explicitly on every change - the family contract is enforced by convention and code review rather than by the framework. Choose this variant only in UIKit codebases; SwiftUI's environment and preference machinery replaces the whole structure.
variants.idiom_name: container UIViewController/UIView subclass owns the model; children report back through delegates or closures
pitfalls: Child view controllers must be added with addChild before their views and removed with removeFromParent, or the hierarchy leaks across navigation.
Delegates and closures are the only channels back to the parent - a child that caches its own copy of the state drifts out of sync after the first change.
State and layout update in separate passes: forgetting setNeedsLayout (or an explicit restyle) after a selection change shows stale styling.
